name: 06-cosimulation
title: Dynamic Coupling — bidirectional co-simulation and physiological intervention

parent_studies.rationale: Intervention acts on the sepsis mechanism fidelity establishes (detect discrepancy -> test treatment).

question:
Can the simulation core run a genuine co-simulation — two processes that exchange
state on every tick inside one composite — rather than running engines in parallel
and comparing them afterwards (studies 01/02) or as parallel tiers (study 03)?
objective:
Demonstrate the co-simulation pillar with a clinically meaningful instance: couple
the real BioGears-sepsis physiology engine (Tellurium) to a closed-loop antibiotic
controller process in one composite, with a feedback edge, and show the loop acting
on the physiology in flight. Run a matched untreated control from the identical
composite (controller disabled).
claim:
The `sepsis_cosim` composite couples two process-bigraph processes that exchange
state every tick. The Tellurium sepsis physiology engine writes its global parameters
(pathogen, hemodynamics) to a shared store. An antibiotic-PK controller process reads
the pathogen, integrates a one-compartment drug PK, and writes the drug-killed
pathogen back into the engine through its `parameters_in` port before the engine's
next step. The treatment the controller computes at tick n changes the physiology the
engine integrates at tick n+1 — a real feedback loop, not two independent runs. With
the controller enabled (closed-loop antibiotic), bacteremia is cleared. With it
disabled (treat=False, the matched control from the same composite), bacteremia
climbs. The pathogen drives septic collapse, so the loop removes the cause. The
multi-day clinical endpoint itself (studies 03/05) is beyond this run's horizon.

expected_behavior.name: two-processes-exchange-state-each-tick
expected_behavior.statement: One composite contains a physiology engine and a controller process wired in a feedback loop (engine.parameters -> controller -> engine.parameters_in); both advance at the same interval and hand state back and forth every tick.

expected_behavior.name: closed-loop-treatment-clears-the-pathogen
expected_behavior.statement: With the controller enabled, the sensed-and-dosed antibiotic drives bacteremia down relative to the matched untreated control run from the identical composite.

expected_behavior.name: treatment-timing-counterfactuals
expected_behavior.statement: Untreated, early-treatment, and delayed-treatment arms from the identical composite give ordered, consistent intervention responses (early clears bacteremia, delayed lets it accumulate first then clears it, untreated climbs).

expected_behavior.name: coupling-step-convergence
expected_behavior.statement: Running the coupled composite at shrinking step sizes (240/120/60 s per tick) changes the endpoint negligibly, so the co-simulation is numerically consistent — execution success is separate from pharmacological credibility.

findings.summary: A physiology engine and an antibiotic controller co-step in one composite, exchanging state every tick.
findings.detail:
The `sepsis_cosim` composite wires two processes into a feedback loop:
  * physiology — the real BioGears-sepsis core run by the Tellurium engine. It
    writes every global parameter (pathogen PT/PB, MAP, SVR, tissue integrity)
    to the shared `parameters` store each step and reads a `parameters_in`
    writeback before the next step.
  * controller — AntibioticControllerProcess: reads `parameters`, senses the
    blood pathogen PB, integrates a one-compartment antibiotic PK (first-order
    elimination), computes an Emax bactericidal kill, and writes the reduced
    PT/PB back to `parameters_in`.
PT/PB are rate-rule state variables in the SBML, not assignment-rule outputs, so
roadrunner accepts the controller's mid-run writeback and the loop closes on the
real flagship model with no model surgery. This is co-simulation in the strict
sense: the controller's tick-n output is the engine's tick-(n+1) input. The same
composite with treat=False makes the controller inert, giving the matched
untreated control.

findings.summary: Closed-loop antibiotic clears bacteremia; the untreated control's pathogen climbs (see chart 01).
findings.detail:
Run at severity 3 over 2 h (120 ticks; see chart 01 and out/cosim_arms.json). The
untreated arm's blood pathogen rises to ~10.6 and plateaus. The closed-loop arm
drives it to 0 once the controller senses PB crossing its trigger and starts the
infusion (final bacteremia ratio untreated/treated = ∞). The treated arm's
sawtooth is the per-tick coupling made visible: the pathogen regrows within each
physiology step and the controller knocks it back down every tick. The figure also
shows the controller's own live state — antibiotic concentration from its
one-compartment PK, rising to ~5.9, and the sensed treat-on flag — which confirms
the second process is simulating, not scripted. Even at this short horizon a
downstream clinical effect is already visible: untreated tissue integrity has
begun to fall (1.000 -> 0.983) while the treated arm holds at 1.000, the first
measurable tissue damage, prevented by clearing the pathogen. Honest limit: the
clinical endpoint that defines septic shock (MAP < 65 mmHg at ~54 h, tissue
integrity minimum 0.24 at 72 h; studies 03/05) is a 2–3 day process, and the exact
engine runs ~1.75 h of wall per simulated 48 h. So this run's horizon shows the
controlled variable (pathogen) and the live PK — the loop removing the cause of
collapse — not the multi-day outcome itself. A full-horizon treated-vs-untreated
endpoint comparison is the natural follow-up.
findings.statement: This co-simulation demonstrates the mechanism (per-tick state exchange with feedback) and the controlled variable (pathogen clearance), not the multi-day clinical endpoint.
findings.explanation: The main claim is a capability claim, and it is fully supported: two process-bigraph processes run in one composite and exchange state every tick through shared stores, with a genuine feedback edge (the controller's writeback at tick n is the engine's input at tick n+1). That is what sets co-simulation apart from the parallel engine comparison of studies 01/02 (same spec under different engines, compared after the fact) and from the parallel surrogate tier of study 03. The clinical instance — a closed-loop antibiotic that senses bacteremia and doses against it — is chosen so the coupling does something legible: the controller clears the pathogen that the matched untreated control (the identical composite with the controller disabled) lets climb. This study does not claim a validated clinical outcome. The pathogen is the upstream driver of the sepsis cascade (inflammation -> vasodilation -> hypotension), so clearing it removes the cause of collapse, but the collapse itself unfolds over 37-72 h (studies 03/05), and the exact engine is too slow to integrate matched treated/untreated arms to that endpoint in this pass. So the honest reading is: the co-simulation capability is demonstrated end to end on the real model, and the treatment's effect on its direct target (bacteremia) is shown; the downstream multi-day endpoint is referenced from the committed severity studies, not re-derived here. The controller's PK is an illustrative Emax/one-compartment model, not a calibrated pharmacology. Swapping it for a COPASI/Tellurium PK engine (true heterogeneous engine-to-engine co-simulation) is a noted follow-up.

findings.summary: Untreated vs early vs delayed treatment give an ordered, consistent response — earlier is better (see chart 02).
findings.detail:
Three arms from the identical sepsis_cosim composite (severity 3, 2 h; delay 1 h),
differing only in when the controller starts (run_counterfactuals.py ->
out/cosim_counterfactuals.json):
  * untreated — bacteremia climbs to 10.6; tissue integrity ends 0.9828.
  * delayed treatment (onset 1 h) — bacteremia tracks the untreated arm for the
    first hour, then drops sharply once treatment starts, ending 0.162; tissue
    integrity ends 0.9874.
  * early treatment (onset at detection) — bacteremia is cleared (ends 0.006);
    tissue integrity holds at 1.0000.
The ordering is consistent: earlier treatment clears the pathogen sooner and
leaves more tissue intact (early 1.0000 > delayed 0.9874 > untreated 0.9828 at 2 h).
The tissue-integrity gaps are small at this horizon because the clinical collapse
is a multi-day process; the pathogen trajectories separate the three arms cleanly.
This is a treatment counterfactual, not a dosing recommendation: the PK is
illustrative, not calibrated.

findings.summary: The co-simulation is numerically consistent: the endpoint converges as the coupling step shrinks.
findings.detail:
Running the early-treatment arm at shrinking coupling steps (240 / 120 / 60 s per
tick, 1 h; out/cosim_convergence.json) gives final bacteremia 0.4115 / 0.3747 /
0.3566 — monotone and converging, a total spread of 0.0548 across a 4× change in
step size (small against the untreated arm's ~10.6). The one-tick coupling lag
shrinks with the step, as expected for operator-split co-simulation. This separates
execution success (the coupling runs and converges) from pharmacological credibility
(the controller's PK is illustrative, not calibrated).
